title: The Market 2026-07 – International Nickel Study Group
text:
The Market 2026-07 – International Nickel Study Group

This article was published in the “Stainless Steel World Magazine”, Volume 38, June 2026

# The World Nickel Market in 2026 – Indonesia, the Influencer

Government and industry representatives met on the 20th and 21st April 2026 for the most recent International Nickel Study Group meetings during which the Group reviewed its forecasts for nickel production and use in 2026.

This article gives a brief overview of recent developments and is based on the data finalized at the meetings.

By Ricardo Ferreira, INSG Director of Market Research and Statistics & Francisco Pinto, INSG Manager of Statistical Analysis

Global growth demonstrated resilience in 2025, supported by AI-related investment and fiscal and monetary policy measures across leading economies. However, the escalation of tensions in the Middle East in late February 2026 is exerting pressure on energy markets and inflation expectations, and global growth is now projected to slow in 2026. How metals markets will ultimately be affected, in terms of production and usage, is still taking shape.

The International Nickel Study Group (INSG) revised its global nickel market outlook at its April 2026 meetings, projecting a surplus of 283 thousand tonnes (kt) for 2025. Estimated primary nickel production for the year reached 3.88 million tonnes (Mt) against usage of 3.596Mt. The picture shifts for 2026, where preliminary data suggest a market deficit of 32kt, as output is expected to fall to 3.715Mt while demand climbs to 3.747Mt.

Source: INSG (Meetings April 2026)

## Nickel mine Production

World nickel mine production declined by 0.8% in 2024, before rebounding by 11.2% in 2025. It is projected to decline again by 5.6% in 2026.

Indonesia continues to dominate global nickel mining, contributing an estimated 65% of world output in 2025 – a share expected to ease to around 62% in 2026. The country’s rapid production growth over the past decade reflects the scale of Chinese-backed investment, which has driven broad capacity additions across intermediate products, such as nickel matte and mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP), as well as primary products such as nickel pig iron (NPI), nickel sulphate, and nickel cathode. Looking ahead, recently announced government policies – RKAB mining quotas and new HPM pricing mechanism – are expected to weigh on the market, introducing a degree of uncertainty into the outlook.

The approved RKAB mining quota has been set in the range of 250-270 Mt – down sharply from 379 Mt in 2025 – with only around 210 Mt having received formal approval as of early April. The approval process itself has tightened considerably, shifting from a three-year to an annual cycle while extending in duration from weeks to several months. Against domestic ore consumption of approximately 280 Mt in 2025, this may create a supply gap. That said, the deficit may be partially offset: Indonesia recorded higher year-on-year (y-o-y) ore imports in the first months of 2026, and additional supply could emerge from ore previously directed toward halted ferronickel operations. Miners retain the option to apply for upward quota revisions around mid-year, making this a key variable to monitor through the second half of the year.

Indonesia’s revised nickel ore benchmark pricing mechanism (HPM), effective 15 April 2026, fundamentally changes how ore costs are assessed. For the first time, the formula incorporates cobalt, iron, and chromium content: cobalt above a 0.05% threshold incurs an additional charge, while iron and chromium are priced at coefficients of 30% and 10%, respectively. This added complexity means that, for any given nickel grade, ore pricing now falls within a range rather than a single figure. While saprolite prices are not expected to shift substantially, limonite grades – whose cobalt content typically meets the charge threshold – are the most affected, with certain grades possibly more than doubling in price. Prior to the HPM revision, ore prices had already been trending upward, though the impact on downstream production remained limited: NPI output declined, but increased matte production from NPI kept total nickel output broadly flat y-o-y in early 2026. Looking ahead, the combination of the revised pricing mechanism and reduced RKAB quotas introduces further uncertainty, with constrained ore availability potentially weighing on production for the rest of the year.

Outside of Indonesia, global nickel mine production in 2025 showed varied performance across regions. The Americas posted solid growth of 9.9%, led by Brazil (+19.0%) and Canada (+14.1%), partially offset by declines in Colombia and Cuba. Asia ex-Indonesia was broadly stable, with the Philippines growing modestly by 5.9% to 375 kt, while Myanmar ceased production entirely. Africa recovered slightly to 122.8 kt (+3.7%), with Zambia standing out at +8.0%.

Looking ahead to 2026, the world total is forecast to decline 5.6% to 3.902 Mt, with the contraction heavily driven by Indonesia. Outside Indonesia, the picture is more nuanced: Oceania is expected to recover 7.0%, led by New Caledonia (+13.0%) and Solomon Islands (+4.2%), while the Americas continue to grow modestly at +2.7%. Europe and Africa remain broadly stable.

## Primary nickel Production

World primary nickel production, after expanding 4.4% in 2024 and a further 8.1% in 2025, is forecast to reverse course in 2026, contracting by 4.2% to 3.715 Mt.

In Asia, output reached 3.19 Mt in 2025 (+11.1%) and is forecast to decline to 3.03 Mt in 2026 (-4.9%).

Indonesia, the world’s leading primary nickel producer since 2021, raised output to 1.89 Mt in 2025 and is forecast to produce 1.77 Mt in 2026, mainly due to a drop in NPI production owing to tighter feed availability. By 2026, the country is expected to account for around 47.6% of world primary nickel output. Production gains in 2025 were supported by rising output of NPI as well as nickel sulphate and nickel cathode, of which the latter two began production domestically in 2023. The government has suspended approvals for new NPI and MHP projects, directing investment towards higher-value downstream industries.

Sulphur is a critical input for MHP production (an intermediate nickel product), requiring 8–12 tonnes per tonne of output and representing 40–50% of total production costs. Indonesia sources 75–80% of its sulphur from the Middle East, with nearly 50% of global seaborne sulphur transiting the Strait of Hormuz, leaving supply heavily exposed to regional disruption. Several MHP producers have already responded by reducing output. Indonesian sulphur stocks offer limited buffer should the conflict persist, and a prolonged disruption could prove severe, potentially forcing further output curtailments across Indonesia’s HPAL sector.

China (P.R.), the world’s second-largest producer, is projected to account for 29.6% of global production in 2026. The ongoing shift from declining NPI production toward higher cathode output is expected to persist, but at a slower rate. Nickel sulphate production is projected to rebound, driven by the battery sector.

Combined Chinese and Indonesian NPI output reached 2.02 Mt in 2025 and is forecast to ease to 1.95 Mt in 2026. Despite this decline, the two countries remain central to global nickel supply, together accounting for the bulk of world primary production.

The Americas grew in 2025, with output rising 8.7%, but are forecast to decline modestly by 1.3% in 2026, as a decrease in Canada is expected to be only partially offset by higher production in Brazil and the planned restart of FeNix in Guatemala. Similarly, Africa recorded a marginal gain in 2025 (+0.4%) but is projected to decline sharply in 2026 (-13.5%), mainly due to an expected decrease in Ambatovy in Madagascar, while Europe saw a slight decline in 2025 (-1.7%) and is expected to recover marginally in 2026 (+0.4%). Oceania’s production dropped sharply again in 2025 (-37.9%), with a modest stabilisation anticipated in 2026 (+2.5%).

## Primary Nickel Usage

Global nickel consumption has followed a steady upward trajectory since 2009, interrupted only in 2020 when demand edged down by 0.6%. Growth continued in 2025, with usage rising 3.5%, and is forecast to expand a further 4.2% in 2026, with China once again driving the bulk of the absolute increase in both years.

Asia further cemented its position as the dominant consuming region, representing 87.8% of global primary nickel usage in 2025 and is forecast to reach 88.1% in 2026 — a remarkable shift from a 63% share in 2010.

China remained the world’s largest nickel consumer by a considerable margin, accounting for over 65% of global usage in 2025 and is forecast to maintain that share in 2026. Demand grew 4.2% in 2025, underpinned primarily by the stainless steel (STS) sector, and is forecast to rise a further 4.3% in 2026. The battery segment is expected to regain momentum in 2026 after contributing at a somewhat reduced pace in 2025.

Indonesia started STS production in 2017 and by 2020 had overtaken Japan to become the world’s second-largest nickel consumer. After surging to 383 kt in 2021, demand contracted in 2022 and 2023 as several countries imposed import restrictions on STS. A recovery followed in 2024, and consumption rose a further 5.3% in 2025. It is forecast to grow 10.3% in 2026. The country is also pursuing a broader objective of developing a downstream battery and EV industry, with nickel expected to play a central role. In Europe, demand has been under pressure, contracting in 2024 and falling a further 2.3% in 2025, before a modest recovery of 1.1% is forecast for 2026.

The Americas recorded growth of 4.3% in 2025, led by the United States where demand rose 4.9%, and consumption is forecast to expand a further 2.7% in 2026, with the US again expected to be the primary driver.

Africa saw usage dip 4.8% in 2025, but a strong rebound of 21.2% is forecast for 2026, supported by a new battery plant in Morocco that came online in 2025 and is poised to lift regional demand in the years ahead.

At the end-use level, the STS sector remains the dominant first-use market for primary nickel, accounting for more than two thirds of total consumption, and was the primary driver of nickel demand growth in both 2024 and 2025. This is expected to remain the case in 2026, with China continuing to lead global STS production growth and Indonesia emerging as an increasingly significant producer. In China, STS production is expected to be supported by infrastructure and machinery demand, continued export growth, and the increasing use of scrap as a cost-efficient and lower-carbon alternative to NPI.

In Europe, STS production is expected to recover in 2026, with any gains driven more by import constraints than underlying demand, supported by the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and a potential mid-2026 quota reduction. In the United States, STS production rose in 2025, underpinned by Section 232 tariffs, though demand has softened since late 2025.

Nickel consumption in EV batteries softened in 2025, with the sector falling short of earlier expectations. LFP chemistry continued to advance, as a number of European and North American OEMs shifted towards these batteries for entry-level and mid-range models, and the technology held an 80% share of domestic installations in China. A broader consumer trend away from full battery EVs and towards plug-in hybrids weighed additionally on nickel demand. Solid-state batteries remain at the pilot stage and are not expected to have any meaningful bearing on nickel demand in 2026.
